description: I Am The Cavalry talks from BSides Las Vegas 2024.

talks.title: Blood in the Water: Preparing For the Feeding Frenzy
talks.teaser: Explores how water utilities face cyber-physical risk, cascading outages and supply chain strain from state-linked attacks.
talks.summary:
Dean Ford, an automation engineer and professional engineer who works on operational technology, opens by framing the water sector as a set of local, loosely connected utilities. He describes patchwork databases, aging pipes and older control equipment, and cites recent documented intrusions into US water systems as a reason for concern.

The middle of the talk becomes a walk through cascading failure. Starting from a simple hotel power outage, the audience works through what breaks next, from air conditioning and elevators to refrigerated medicine and evacuation. The same chain is then applied to a compromised pump controller. Long replacement lead times, thin spare inventories and reliance on a single vendor turn one device fault into a supply problem. A hypothetical water hammer, caused by manipulated pumps or valves, shows how brittle pipes can fail across a network, and the loss of pressure then reaches hospitals, fire protection, airports and data centers.

The closing argues that a proposed sanitary-style cyber assessment was rejected, that utilities are underfunded, and that insurance and single-product purchases can give false comfort. Practical takeaways include knowing where your water comes from and how old the pipes are, planning around outage duration, keeping critical spares, diversifying vendors, and attending local utility meetings. He also stresses that the skills needed to run these systems are more than one person can hold.

talks.title: Health Care is in Intensive Care
talks.teaser: Examines how ransomware on hospitals harms patients, and which policy and technical controls could restore healthcare resilience.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the speaker's path from emergency medicine into healthcare security, using cardiac arrest as a frame. Minutes matter for blood flow to the brain, so delays sharply cut the chance of recovery. The talk argues that hospitals now depend heavily on connected devices, electronic records, cloud services and outside vendors. It traces recent attacks, including incidents at Change Healthcare and Ascension, where clinicians reported paper charts and lost monitoring.

The core evidence is a study of a 2021 ransomware attack on San Diego hospitals. At one hospital across the street from the affected systems, the attack drove up ambulance arrivals, longer waits, and more patients leaving before being seen. County-wide, hospitals spent record hours on ambulance diversion. Cardiac arrest patients who recovered with favorable neurologic function reportedly fell from about 40 percent to roughly 4.5 percent during the attack month. Lost records also made outcomes hard to measure afterward.

The closing argument treats restoration as the CPR of hospital cyber response, where speed matters most. Proposed steps include mapping critical vendors and technologies, joint planning with emergency managers and continuity staff, and replacement systems that can bridge care during an outage. Economic incentives and consolidation are presented as hard problems without easy fixes. The question-and-answer session returned to the lack of good data on hospital attacks and the financial pressures behind them.

talks.title: Hungry, Hungry Hackers
talks.teaser: Traces how farm-equipment bugs became a food-supply security problem for critical infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a researcher's look at a farm-equipment vendor's developer portal, where a form for registering a machine by its identification number returned full customer account records in its response. The vendor had no bug bounty at the time, so the researcher published the finding instead of signing a non-disclosure agreement. Press coverage followed, and the company later launched a bounty and a formal cyber program.

From there the talk widens to the wider agriculture sector. It covers a jailbroken tractor running custom software, a report that equipment seized in Ukraine was disabled remotely, and recent ransomware attacks on a meat processor, grain co-ops, a fuel pipeline and a food producer. It also looks at the split between food and agriculture information-sharing groups, a manufacturer-run cyber tractor challenge, a proposed US farm security bill, and cross-sector dependencies on rail, water, rural healthcare and finance.

The closing takeaways are that vendors should be ready to receive reports even without a bounty, that competitors gain by sharing threat knowledge, and that equipment needs signed firmware updates and unique keys rather than a shared key. In the Q&A, the answers suggested that non-technical people can help by favouring secure products when they buy and by explaining risk in plain terms.

talks.title: Difficult Conversations
talks.teaser: Explores how security professionals could self-organize, drawing on licensing models from other professions.
talks.summary:
Andrea M. Matwyshyn opens by arguing that the security field lacks a shared language and a set of trusted sources that ordinary people and policymakers can rely on. She frames the session around professional societies, explaining why occupations form self-regulatory bodies: to shape a public-facing reputation, to mentor newcomers, and to give members a collective voice when policy goes wrong.

The middle of the session draws on historical cases. A dam collapse that ignored engineers' warnings contributed to the formation of engineering societies and codes of ethics, and environmental crises pushed legislators toward clean air and water laws. She compares how fields such as law, medicine, financial advisers, and cosmetology handle licensing, exams, continuing education, insurance, sponsorship, and sanctions for misconduct. She also floats the idea of a "chief technology safety officer" role, a peer position inside organizations that could push back on unsafe releases.

In the question period, attendees raised concerns about membership costs, how the public can judge a practitioner's competence, the risk of regulatory capture, and whether a certification could be objective enough to be meaningful. The answers stressed starting small with shared values and bottom-up roundtables rather than waiting for government action. The session closed with the view that doing nothing is not an acceptable path as systems grow more interdependent.

talks.title: Living With the Enemy - How to protect yourself (and Energy Systems)
talks.teaser: Covers protecting yourself and energy systems while living with the enemy.

talks.title: Security Trek: The Next Generation
talks.teaser: Argues that security education should emphasize process, open-source tooling, and hands-on experience over buying products.
talks.summary:
The speaker looks back at the early days of public security outreach, when mainstream audiences had little understanding of information security or privacy. Awareness has improved since then, the argument goes, but the next challenge is turning that concern into concrete protective action. Small organizations often cannot afford in-house security staff, and graduates with security degrees frequently struggle to land jobs without practical experience.

The central message is that security depends more on process than on products. The speaker advises listeners to judge vendors by whether they focus on investor growth rather than customers, and suggests calling a vendor's sales team with technical questions to see whether anyone knowledgeable answers. Generic awareness training that covers outdated attacks is criticized, and the talk pushes back on the misconception that open source means exposed data. Star Trek episodes serve as analogies for explaining incidents to lay people.

The talk then describes a volunteer program that refurbishes donated computers, installs a Linux Mint build configured to CIS controls, and teaches students and their parents about privacy and security, while giving volunteers real-world experience. The speaker notes that Nevada recognized CIS controls as a definition of reasonable security, and recommends that listeners use that reference to justify process-focused spending to management.

talks.title: Wars and Rumors of Wars - What are the implications for Domestic Critical Infrastructure?
talks.teaser: Walks through a hypothetical pre-positioned attack on US critical infrastructure and asks how communities can prepare.
talks.summary:
Karl Holmqvist and Beau Woods open a session under I Am The Cavalry that treats the line between war and peace as blurry. They draw on a 1999 Chinese military text on unrestricted warfare and on examples of economic, legal and psychological pressure to argue that a state adversary may already be operating in a conflict-like posture against domestic infrastructure.

The core of the talk is a tabletop scenario set on a late December night in 2026, when pre-positioned malware in IT networks activates across water, power, telecommunications, healthcare and transportation. The audience works through the timeline hour by hour. They discuss how utilities without central coordination would see pressure surges and outages as isolated faults, how telecom and emergency dispatch degrade, how hospitals lose function without water, and how fabricated media and public pressure could slow decisions. The presenters add a possible Taiwan invasion running alongside to delay a US military response.

The closing discussion turns to preparation. Participants suggested local drills, getting to know neighbors and emergency managers, sharing intelligence through sector groups, making disclosure easier for researchers, funding defenders and reducing dependence on connected systems. The session stresses that psychological harm can outlast physical damage, and that practical readiness for disruption matters more than waiting for new regulation.

talks.title: Cybersec and AI Risk Management Challenges for the Next Generation of Public Safety Systems
talks.teaser: Explains how public safety agencies can adopt connected and AI systems with workable cyber risk management and outside help.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the concern that public safety agencies, including fire, police, emergency dispatch and the private contractors that serve them, are adopting connected and AI-enabled systems while having little cybersecurity or AI expertise. The speaker argues that vendors often blur definitions, and that artificial intelligence covers many techniques beyond modern deep learning, so agencies need a clear scope before they buy. Next Generation 911, search robots, drones and wildland fire tools were used as examples, along with a ransomware incident that hit a city's 911 system after a contractor removed a firewall to make something work.

The middle section focuses on risk management. In this setting, risk management means reducing the chance of serious harm rather than eliminating risk, and practitioners should weigh technical impact against the likelihood of acceptance, understanding and actionability. Interoperability problems, such as responders from different agencies needing a shared device with unfamiliar credentials, show why standard corporate policies often do not fit. Long equipment lifecycles of around fifteen years also make retrofitting costly and slow.

To close, the speaker urged the security community to take part in public comment on standards and frameworks, write guidance that flags exceptions for unusual use cases, and speak through the channels agencies already follow, such as trade shows and podcasts. Vendors were encouraged to say when a product is unsuitable for a given purpose. In the audience discussion, a speaker noted that audit cycles and grant requirements may give outsiders an opening to offer help, and another pointed out that agencies often do not know which questions to ask.

talks.title: Time is up. You have three years, 3 months, 3 weeks, to protect your Stuff. What do you do?
talks.teaser: Explores short-term steps communities and operators can take to reduce risk from disruptive attacks on critical infrastructure.
talks.summary:
This session opens a two-hour discussion of how to reduce risk to critical infrastructure when a destructive attack seems close, with the focus on measures that work within months rather than years. Josh Corman frames the problem around recent disruptions in healthcare, water, food, energy and pipelines, and around government warnings about a state-linked campaign already present in US utilities. The central concern is the cascading effect of a destructive attack, not a ransom, and the talk stresses that many operators lack staff, budget and basic know-how to respond.

The middle portion covers the policy picture. A White House representative describes a national cyber strategy that is moving from voluntary guidance toward using existing regulatory authority. Topics include sector-by-sector risk identification, the CISA baseline performance goals and its list of bad practices, and efforts to identify systemically important entities. Healthcare serves as the main example: losing medical technology and staff raises mortality for time-sensitive care, and a hospital closing after a prolonged disruption is a lasting harm to its region.

The closing discussion turns to near-term actions. Suggested steps include removing unnecessary internet-facing services, fixing known exploited vulnerabilities first, eliminating default credentials, and keeping analog fallbacks such as manual procedures and water filtration. Audience questions covered workforce pipelines, accreditation bodies, federal grants and local tabletop exercises. The main takeaway is that much of near-term resilience comes from simplifying systems and building community capacity rather than adding new tools.

talks.title: Introduction to I Am The Cavalry - Preparing for 2027
talks.teaser: Recaps the prior day and frames the critical-infrastructure risks, Volt Typhoon concerns and planned 2027 preparedness work.
talks.summary:
The session opens the second day of the I Am The Cavalry track with a recap of the first day's themes. The speaker argues that society depends on connected technology that is not dependable, and that disruptions to lifeline services are growing larger, longer and more likely to affect safety. Healthcare payment systems, a non-malicious software update that caused widespread outages, and rural hospitals with only a few weeks of cash reserves are used as examples of how a single failure can cascade.

The middle of the talk focuses on Volt Typhoon, described as pre-positioning inside US water utilities, and on the possibility of destructive action around 2027. The speaker points out that many small operators in rural areas lack security staff and cannot follow standard frameworks, so practical steps matter more than long programs. The talk also introduces a one-year pilot called Undisrupted 27, which concentrates on water, food, emergency care and power, and proposes informing, influencing and inspiring people through tested messaging rather than technical advice alone.

The closing section asks attendees to consider their own household readiness for a water or power interruption, and previews the discussion blocks later in the day on preparedness, wartime rumors and the pilot's work. The main takeaway is that near-term preparation, honest communication and community resilience are the practical priorities while longer-term fixes take years to arrive.

talks.title: Getting Serious (Un)-Resilience of Lifeline Critical Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Frames the growing risk to food, water, healthcare and energy services, and how disruptions could cascade across them.
talks.summary:
Josh Corman opens the I Am The Cavalry track at BSidesLV 2024 by looking back at the group's origins and the widening gap between dependence on connected technology and the ability to secure it. He argues that disruptions to lifeline sectors such as food, water, healthcare and energy are becoming larger and longer, and that accidents as well as adversaries can cause serious public harm. He points to hospital finances as an example, noting that cash-flow outages from ransomware and rural hospital closures can cut off timely care for whole communities.

The middle of the talk turns to the possibility of a destructive conflict. Corman reviews public US government testimony about the Volt Typhoon campaign, which he describes as pre-positioning inside critical infrastructure, and treats it as a planning scenario for a hybrid conflict. He explains how quickly a loss of water would shut down a hospital's core functions, and he previews the day's speakers covering food, water, hospitals and municipal power. He also outlines a one-year pilot that uses plain, creative communication to reach local operators and residents before 2027.

He closes by urging the audience to identify systemically important entities, prepare with tabletop exercises, and take simple resilience steps for households and towns within a short time frame. The practical takeaway is that the work is about keeping essential services running during a disruption, not only protecting data.
